claims.text: The alloy has a lamellar multiphase FCC/B2 microstructure.
Pre-oxidation at the test temperature produces an initially protective oxide layer.
Accelerated coupled degradation arises from a synergistic tribo-oxidation mechanism.
Sliding wear dynamically disrupts and removes the protective oxide film.
Oxide-film removal exposes fresh FCC/B2 phase boundaries.
Exposed FCC/B2 phase boundaries act as microgalvanic cells that accelerate local corrosion.
Corrosion preferentially attacks the less noble phase at FCC/B2 interfaces.
Localized corrosion softens the less noble phase at the interfaces.
Corrosion-induced interfacial softening increases material removal by wear.
The reciprocal effects of wear and corrosion form a positive feedback loop.
Simultaneous wear-corrosion produces total degradation greater than the additive sum of the separate processes.
Total mass loss during simultaneous exposure will be more than 100% greater than the sum of the wear-only and corrosion-only mass losses.
Wear volume during simultaneous exposure will increase by 20% relative to wear-only exposure.
Corrosion current density during simultaneous exposure will increase by 200% relative to corrosion-only exposure.
Oxide-film thickness and integrity at FCC/B2 boundaries and lamellar-interface density are the relevant structural mediators.
The proposed mechanism applies to lamellar eutectic HEAs in chloride electrolytes at sliding loads of 5–20 N and temperatures of 400–600 °C.
The proposed mechanism is not expected to hold for single-phase alloys or nonchloride environments.
The proposed mechanism is not expected to hold during static immersion without mechanical action.

contradictions.description: A fully immersed aqueous 3.5 wt% NaCl test at 500 °C and ambient pressure is internally incompatible: the aqueous electrolyte cannot remain a conventional liquid at that temperature without substantial pressurization or a different molten-salt formulation.

The baseline requires separate tests under identical electrolyte conditions, but the specified wear-only control is dry sliding and therefore does not have the same electrolyte condition as the simultaneous test.
The baseline calls for identical load and speed in the corrosion-only test, whereas the corrosion-only design is static immersion and has no sliding load or speed.
The predictions specify increases of 20% and 200%, but the falsification rule treats values equal to those predicted margins as failures by using ≤20% and ≤200%.
